heading: NSABP Studies: An Overview
full_text: See [Bernard Fisher: 1918-2019]. Summaries in quotations below are cited directly from the [50 years of NSABP Website]. 1970s "Was the disfiguring surgery more effective than the breast-conserving procedures being proposed by some surgeons? The trials that ultimately answered this question were begun in 1971 with [NSABP B-04], which, after 25 years of follow-up, continued to demonstrate no difference in recurrence or survival among patients with operable breast cancer treated with either breast-conserving procedures or radical mastectomy. The results of the B-04 trial were so significant that in 1979 the NIH Consensus Conference announced that mastectomy and axillary dissection should be considered the standard treatment for early breast cancer, resulting in the rapid decline in radical mastectomy. Succeeding clinical trials gave even more credence to the hypothesis that breast-conserving surgery results were at least as good as those for the more radical procedure." [NSABP B-06] compared BCS, BCT and TM with ALND for all. There was a small DCIS cohort in this trial. 1980s "During the 1980's, mammography became widely used, making it possible for physicians to diagnose very small tumors. [NSABP B-17] was developed to determine if DCIS, tumors too small to be felt, could be treated using tissue-conserving techniques. Lumpectomy alone (BCS) was compared to lumpectomy plus radiation (BCT) in patients with localized disease. The results of this landmark study demonstrated that radiation therapy significantly reduced the incidence of cancer in the ipsilateral breast, marking another step forward by the NSABP in a decade that was memorable for advancements in breast cancer research." Notable NSABP DCIS trials: B-06, B-17, B-24. [NSABP B-14] was the first characterization of tamoxifen benefits/side effects. It was developed to determine if IDC tumors in ER(+) women with histologically negative lymph nodes would benefit from tamoxifen. [NSABP B-20] later evaluated the benefit in the addition of chemo to tamoxifen in this subgroup. These two trials are what [Oncotype Dx] is based upon. [NSABP B-24] evaluated the natural history of DCIS with or without Tamoxifen in the setting of BCT (standard per B-17), demonstrating around 3% absolute risk reduction in both ipsilateral (30% RRR) and contralateral (50% RRR) breast tumor recurrence. Note: Only 75% of patients were ER+ on this trial, so the RRR for IBTR with tamoxifen may be under-stated. [NSABP B-21] was developed to determine if IDC, tumors too small to be felt, would benefit from tamoxifen alone vs. WBRT vs. WBRT + Tamoxifen after breast conserving surgery (BCS). Long term follow-up questioned the benefit in IBTR when adding tamoxifen in the setting of WBRT, especially for small tumors. However, it proved a 3% decrease in contralateral breast tumors with tamoxifen. Notably, only 56% of patients in this study were ER+ (i.e., stood less of a chance to see benefit in IBTR with tamoxifen), so the benefit of hormone blockers in the setting of BCT [remains in question]. 1990s and Chemoprevention "The group maintained its focus during this difficult period, and its first chemoprevention study, the first breast cancer chemoprevention trial ever conducted, was launched in 1992. In [NSABP P-1], more than 13,000 well women, determined to be at increased risk of developing breast cancer, were randomly assigned to tamoxifen or a placebo. After 5 years, there was a 49% reduction in invasive breast cancer in the group taking tamoxifen. In the [NSABP P-2 (STAR)], a trial of nearly 20,000 women, that opened at the end of the decade, tamoxifen and raloxifene were shown to be equally effective in reducing the risk of invasive breast cancer, with fewer cardiovascular side effects in those women taking raloxifene." 1990s and Neoadjuvant vs. Adjuvant Chemo [NSABP B-18] and [B-27] proved neoadjuvant chemotherapy to have equivalent DFS/OS to adjuvant chemotherapy, and may convert to breast conserving surgery. The addition of a taxol in the preoperative setting appears to double pathologic complete response rate. 2000s "In the 15 years that followed (the turn of the century), the results of the NSABP [B-31] and [B-32] trials changed the way breast cancer was treated and established a new standard of care. [B-31] demonstrated that the addition of 52 weeks of Herceptin to standard therapy reduced mortality by 39%, findings that excited the oncology community worldwide. [B-32]  resolved a question that had been asked for many years: Could results from sentinel node resection equal those from conventional axillary dissection in clinically node-negative breast cancer patients? After more than 10 years of follow-up, there continues to be no significant difference in overall survival or in disease-free survival for the study patients, making it possible for them to avoid a more extensive surgical procedure with its associated increased risks" "In 2014, under the NCI mandate to reduce the number of National Clinical Trials groups, the NSABP joined with the Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) and Gynecological Oncology Group (GOG), to create a new corporation qualified to become the federal grantee. Government-sponsored breast and colon studies led by the NSABP are now developed and managed within the NRG Oncology Foundation, Inc." Future Directions [NSABP B-39] has demonstrated the safety and efficacy of APBI, while [NSABP B-51] is an ongoing trial evaluating patients with a cN+ axilla at diagnosis who develop a negative SLNB after NAC.

heading: EBCTCG Studies: An Overview
full_text: Summaries in quotations below are cited directly from the [EBCTCG Previous Findings Website]. 2005 "The report on [Surgery and Radiotherapy] showed that regimens that substantially reduce 5-year local recurrence rates have little effect on 5-year breast cancer mortality, but moderately reduce 15-year breast cancer mortality.” Origin of 4:1 rule. "The Lancet report on [Systemic Therapies] showed the substantial effects on 15y survival of the chemo regimens (eg, about 6 mos of anthracycline-based chemo) and endocrine regimens (eg, 5 years of tamoxifen) that were being tested in the 1980s." 2010 IBTR halved with RT for [DCIS] (compared to [2/3 RRR] with RT in addition to BCS for IDC). Around half of recurrences are invasive. There is no difference in BCM or OM. However, no therapy has demonstrated an OS benefit for DCIS given the [low risk of death] to begin with. The benefit for BCT in DCIS is more pronounced in women < 50y. 2011 "The 2011-12 Lancet reports updated evidence from 2005, bringing together data from 100,000 women in 123 randomized trials of [chemotherapy], showing that chemotherapy can reduce breast cancer mortality not only in ER-negative but also in ER-positive disease, and showing benefits of taxane-based over standard anthracycline chemotherapy." “The 2011 report on radiotherapy after [breast-conserving surgery] showed that radiotherapy halves the rate at which the disease recurs and reduces the breast cancer death rate by about a sixth.” 2012 “The 2012 report on 20,000 women in 20 RCTs of about 5y of [tamoxifen] versus no tamoxifen, showed a highly significant reduction of about a third in BCM not only during years 0-4 and 5-9 after starting treatment but also during years 10-14. Tamoxifen is effective whether or not chemotherapy has been given and, importantly, even in weakly ER positive [low positive] disease.” 2014 “The 2014 report showed that after mastectomy, [PMRT + RNI] reduced breast cancer recurrence and mortality not only in women whose breast cancer had spread to many lymph nodes but also in those with spread to only 1-3 ALNs” 2015 "The 2015 report on 20,000 women in 26 randomized trials of [bisphosphonates], showed that 2–5 years of treatment with these drugs, which are usually used to treat osteoporosis, reduces the risk of breast cancer recurring in the bones, and significantly extends survival. However, bisphosphonate treatment appears effective only for post-menopausal women and has little effect in premenopausal women." “The 2015 report on 30,000 postmenopausal women in 9 randomized trials comparing [aromatase inhibitors] (AIs) with tamoxifen, showed that 5y of treatment with an AI produces even better survival than 5y of tamoxifen. Compared to tamoxifen, taking AIs for 5y further reduced the likelihood of the cancer recurring by 30%, and the risk of dying from breast cancer by around 15%. Thus taking an AI for 5y, compared to no endocrine treatment, would reduce the risk of dying from breast cancer by around 40% in the decade after starting treatment.” 2017 “A 2017 report on the [20-year risks of breast cancer recurrence after stopping endocrine therapy after 5 years] showed that when endocrine therapy ended, the risk of the cancer reappearing and spreading throughout the body continued at a similar rate over at least the next 15 years. The risk depended mainly on the original cancer’s size, and the number of lymph nodes that were cancerous. But, even for those patients with the best outlook (small tumors with no spread to the lymph nodes), there was a 10% chance of cancer spread 20 years after the initial diagnosis, sufficient for further endocrine therapy to be at least considered” "Report on the [risks of breast cancer radiotherapy] included more than 40,000 women in 75 randomized trials and showed that late side-effects of modern radiation therapy for breast cancer depend largely on a woman’s smoking status. For non-smokers, the absolute risks of lung cancer and heart disease from modern radiation therapy were < 1%. But for long-term continuing smokers they were close to 5%, which may outweigh the benefit. Stopping smoking at the time of radiotherapy may avoid much of this risk." 2018 “The 2018 report on 4500 women in 10 trials of [neoadjuvant chemotherapy] versus adjuvant chemotherapy showed that there was no significant difference between neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy for distant recurrence, breast cancer mortality or death from any cause. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy allowed more women to have breast-conserving therapy than adjuvant chemotherapy. However, the risk of cancer recurring in the breast or adjacent lymph glands (local recurrence) was somewhat higher in the neoadjuvant than the adjuvant chemotherapy group. This increased risk of local recurrence was greater in trials which omitted surgery in the event of a good response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.” 2019 “The 2019 report on 37,000 women in 26 trials of [chemotherapy dose intensification] showed that increasing dose intensity (e.g. by 2-weekly rather than 3-weekly administration) reduced the risk of breast cancer recurrence and death.” 2023 The 2023 report on 14,000 women in 16 trials of [RT to regional nodes in early breast cancer] showed that regional nodal irradiation significantly reduces breast cancer mortality and all cause mortality in trials done after the 1980s, but not in older trials. These contrasted findings could reflect RT improvements since the 1980s.

heading: General
full_text: Staging Tables updated from the 2017 ARRO study guide. Instant.Oncology: Breast Cancer [Staging], [Risk Factors], and [Carcinogenesis]. New in 2010: IA and IB based upon the presence of micromets. pN1mi - 0.2-2 mm; ITC if < 0.2 mm (N0). ITC: ≤ 0.2 mm; behave like pN0. Micromets (> 0.2-2 mm) have a prognosis between pN0 and macromets pN1. New in 2018: Prognostic staging, as HR- and TNBC do worse. HER2+ intermediate prognosis. Get the AJCC 8th ed Breast Cancer Staging App (including prognostic groups) for [iPhone] or [Android]. A note on prognostic stage grouping: T1-2N0 ER+, HER2- downgraded to IA if Oncotype < 11. PR(+) in the setting of ER(+) downswings to IA unless T2G3. Upstaging: T3N1 (IIIA) can't be IIIC if HER2(+), HR(+) or G1. HER2-, HR-, and grade can "upswing" It is common for prognostic staging to "anchor down" if HR is disjointed (i.e., ER+/PR- or ER-/PR+). Downstaging: T3N1 (IIIA) can be pIB if G1-2 and triple positive. If HR is disjointed, no down-swinging allowed even if G1, HER2+ N2b: IM - axilla, N3b IM + axilla. N3 refers to Level III or higher LNs: cN3a - infraclav (Level III); cN3c - SCV. The Landmark Series: Adjuvant RT for Breast Cancer [Valente & Shah, Surg Onc '20] RoR Most frequently dx cancer globally: 250k invasives (80%) and 60k non-invasives (20%) in the U.S. with 40k deaths in 2016. Most commonly diagnosed: Breast > Lung > CRC. Cause of death: Lung > breast > CRC. 61 median age of dx. Incidence of diagnosis is increasing. Of women born in 2009, ~12% (1 in 8) will be dx with BrCa. ~80% of breast cancer patients are diagnosed with stage 0-II breast cancer. Incidence of T3-4 disease decreased by 27% from 1980-1987. Coincides with the institution of mammography (MMA). SEER analysis from 1992-1999 demonstrated LABC and IBC comprised around 5% and 1% of BrCa. Incidence of mortality has been decreasing. Since 1991, BCM has been declining. Historically more whites had it > 40y, now normalizing 50-59. Risk factors: Female, age, Fhx, early menarche, late menopause older age at first birth, prolonged HRT (RR 1.7), previous RT, increased MMA breast density, BRCA1/2. Only 10% are associated with germline mutations. Prevention: Avoid HRT! HRT with estrogen and progestin is associated with an increased RR of 1.7. HRT Meta [Lancet '19]: Lean women see increases in breast cancer risk with menopausal HRT. Any type of menopausal HRT (except vaginal estrogen) was associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. For example, combination MHT x 5 years in an average weight woman resulted in a 2% absolute increase in breast cancer at 20 years. Estrogen-alone MHT x 5 years resulted in a 0.5% absolute increase in breast cancer at 20 years. These rates roughly double for double the duration. Interestingly, the excess risk from MHT was attenuated by weight—but not how you might think. While lean women saw increases in breast cancer risk with MHT, MHT (particularly estrogen alone) didn’t really seem to increase the already-elevated baseline risk among obese women. TBLQS: Systemic (read: not topical) hormone replacement in postmenopausal women increases the risk of breast cancer in proportion to duration and inverse proportion to BMI. Million Women Study [Beral Lancet '19]: 1/3 of women were taking MHT upon enrollment, while another 15% had a history of MHT. Alas, these women with a history of MHT saw a significant increase in breast cancer mortality over the next 20 years. While the increased risk was seen across all groups, women taking combination MHT for over 5 years had a particularly increased risk. TBLQS: The excess breast cancers associated with prolonged combination menopausal hormone replacement are also associated with an increased risk of breast cancer mortality. The Landmark Series: Adjuvant RT for Breast Cancer [Valente & Shah, Surg Onc '20]: BCT demonstrates a LC and BCM benefit, while PMRT demonstrates improved OS for appropriately selected patients. A must-read review discussing BCT and mastectomy, PMRT, Hypofractionation, adjuvant RT with a positive sentinel lymph node, adjuvant RT with ALND, PBI with BT or 3D, and IORT. Credit: Dr Lei Wang. Click image above or follow @instant.oncology on Instagram. When is a woman menopausal? Instant.Oncology: [Bone remodeling] H/o BSO, Age > 60, Age < 60 and amenorrheic for ≥ 12 months in the absence of therapy.* *If on tamoxifen or toremifene, must have FSH and estradiol in postmenopausal range (i.e. FSH > ~25.8 mIU/mL) Pregnancy Instant.Oncology: [Fertility options for patients] Consider MRI (no CT). Same prognosis as non-pregnant women. 1st trimester: Discuss termination. TM + ALND→ Chemo in 2nd trimester→ delivery→ RT→ Tam. 2nd trimester: Surgery can include BCS and ALND (no SLNB). Non-taxane based chemo in 2nd and 3rd trimesters: FAC most common. FAC: 5-FU, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide. Non-taxane chemo, most common for pregnant women. No Tam/AI or SLN dye during pregnancy. No RT in any trimester. Simplified BRCA Testing Criteria [Mainstream Cancer Genetics], Prospectively validated [Kemp JAMA Onc '19]:Family History is a thing of the past. Relying on complicated family medical trees to decipher who should and shouldn’t be tested for BRCA-mutations has led to some serious undertesting of people at risk. This is due to a couple of reasons: (1) it’s complicated, and (2) patients don’t know their family medical trees. TBLQS: Five simple cancer criteria can be used to identify patients with 10% risk of harboring a BRCA-mutation, making way for a streamlined and cost-effective testing approach with no middle man. MCG BRCA Testing Eligibility Criteria: An individual with any of the following: Ovarian cancer. Breast cancer ≤ 45y. Two primary breast cancers, both ≤ 60y. TNBC. Male breast cancer. ≤ 10% of breast cancers are due to hereditary mutations in a single gene. If BRCAmt, consider annual MMA and MRI breast 10y prior to the youngest family member with breast cancer but not prior to age 30 (MMA) or age 25 (MRI). Also screen younger if RT to chest at a young age (same rules for minimum age of 25y for MRI or 30y for MMA, but 10y after prior thoracic RT). BRCA-CRisk: Estimates CBC in BRCA ½ carriers based on age of first cancer, presence of first degree relative cancer, BRCA variant near the 3' region, and endocrine therapy [Sun JCO '22]. QS USPSTF Guideline: Risk Assessment, Genetic Counseling, and Genetic Testing for BRCA-related cancer [JAMA '19] Breast + Ovarian in one individual. Breast cancer < 50y. Bilateral breast cancer. Male family members with breast cancer. Multiple cases of breast cancer in the family. 1+ family member with 2 primary types of BRCA cancer (such as ovarian, breast, prostate, pancreas cancer). Ashkenazi jew ancestry. Consensus Guidelines on Genetic Testing for Hereditary Breast Cancer from the ASBrS [Manahan ASO '10] Genetic testing should be made available to all patients with a personal history of breast cancer. Testing should include BRCA1/BRCA2, PALB2, P53, ATM, CHEK2, PTEN, CDH1 and STK11. Variants of uncertain significance are not clinically actionable and should be managed on individual risk factors. ASCO/ASTRO/SSO Guideline: Management of Hereditary Breast Cancer QS [Tung JCO '20, Trombetta PRO '20] Newly diagnosed BRCA1/2 mutations may be considered for BCT with local control of the index cancer similar to that of non-carriers. The significant risk of contralateral breast cancer, especially in young women, and the higher risk of new cancers in the ipsilateral breast warrant discussion of bilateral mastectomy. Nipple sparing mastectomy is a reasonable approach. Patients with mutations in moderate-risk genes should be offered BCT. For women with BRCA1/2 or moderate-penetrance genes who are eligible for mastectomy, nipple-sparing mastectomy is a reasonable approach. Radiation should not be withheld in ATM carriers. For patients with germline TP53 mutations, mastectomy is advised; RT is contraindicated except in those with significant risk of LRR. Platinum agents are recommended versus taxanes to treat advanced breast cancer in BRCA carriers. In the adjuvant/neoadjuvant setting, data do not support the routine addition of platinum to anthracycline and taxane-based chemotherapy. PARPi (olaparib and talazoparib) are preferable to non-platinum single-agent chemotherapy for treatment of advanced breast cancer in BRCA1/2 carriers. Data is insufficient to recommend PARPi use in the early setting or in moderate-penetrance cancers. ASCO Hereditary Breast Cancer Guideline Rapid Recommendation Update [Tung JCO '21] Results of [OlympiA] in 2021 now provides evidence for one year of adjuvant olaparib for early-stage HER2- breast cancer with high risk of recurrence and germline BRCA1/2 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants after completion of (neo)adjuvant chemo and local treatment, including RT. Surgery first: 1y adjuvant olaparib should be offered with > 2 cm TNBC or any involved axillary nodes. HR+ disease: 1y adjuvant olaparib should be offered to those with at least four involved axillary lymph nodes. NAC: 1y adjuvant olaparib should be offered to TNBC with residual disease; for HR+ disease, 1y of adjuvant olaparib should be offered to pts with residual disease and a clinical stage, pathologic stage, ER, and tumor grade score ≥ 3 (Table 1).

heading: Genetics
full_text: Genetic Factors in the Locoregional Management of Breast Cancer [Haffty, Euhus and Pierce JCO '20]. StatPearls: BRCA 1 and 2 Last update: 4/21/20. Around 5-10% of breast cancers are due to a heritable mutation. In appropriately selected pts (read: BRCAmt, DNA-DRmt), [PARPi] is promising in the [neoadjuvant] or [metastatic] setting. Testing should include BRCA1/BRCA2, PALB2, P53, ATM, CHEK2, PTEN, CDH1 and STK11 [Manahan ASO '10]. [BRCA testing criteria]: Ovarian, Breast cancer ≤ 45yo, two primary breast cancers ≤ 60yo, TNBC, male breast cancer. TNBC at age ≤ 60 yo will have BRCA-2 in 10% of patients. Male breast cancer: More likely ER+, BRCA 2. Loosest criteria: Three diagnoses of breast cancer at any age within two degrees of relationship. Known mutation in family. Ashkenazi jew: As many as 1 in 40 Ashkenazi jews have BRCA1 or BRCA 2 [Metcalfe JCO '10]. Family member with breast cancer and other cancers in the same person such as prostate, pancreas. Age 45-50 with up to a second degree relative with breast cancer, any age. Breast cancer and relative with breast cancer ≤ 50yo. ≥ 1 ovarian cancer on the same side of the family. ≥ 2 relatives with breast cancer on the same side of the family. BRCA1 behaves like TNBC. More aggressive, more G3. Chromosome 17q. Higher risk for Ovarian and cOlon. ~20% TN will be associated with BRCA, while only 5% of all BrCa associated with BRCA [Gonzalez-Angulo '11]. BRCA2 behaves like sporadic, more likely lobular. HR+, HER2 neg. Chromosome 13q. Pancreatic, prostate, male breast cancer, ovarian, D1 fanconi anemia. ~50% risk of breast, ~20% risk ovarian. Two other hereditary syndromes: Li-Fraumeni (TP53) and Cowden syndrome (PTEN), both are a result of TSGs. Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba is also a mutation of PTEN (TSG). Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer syndrome (Cadherin 1 [CDH1]). BRCA1 vs. 2 [Chen JCO '07]: BRCA1 vs. BRCA2.BRCA1 behaves like TNBC, and has a higher risk of female breast, Ovarian and cOlon cancer than BRCA 2. BRCA2 behaves more like sporadic (HR+), and is more likely to be associated with male breast, prostate, and pancreas cancer. Male breast cancer 1→ 7% [Giordano NEJM '18]. Female breast cancer 60→ 50%. Ovarian cancer 40→ 20%. CIMBA: Pathology of breast and ovarian cancer [Mavaddat Ca Epidem Bio Prev '12]: BRCA1 and BRCA2. Cohort of 6893 females with BRCA pathogenic variants. ER negativity for BRCA1 / 2 of 78→ 23%. TNBC for BRCA1 / 2 of  68→ 16%. These differences partially dissipate with advancing age (Fig 2C/F). Lobular cancers are most likely associated with BRCA2, while medullary cancers are associated with BRCA1. CIMBA: Pathology of male cancers (1966-2017) [Silvestri JAMA Onc '20]: BRCA1 vs. BRCA 2. There are significant differences in the cancer spectrum in males with BRCA2 versus BRCA 1. TBL QS: Men with BRCA1/2 mutations have exceedingly high rates of all kinds of cancers that likely merit especially vigilant education and screening interventions. Cohort of 6,902 males with BRCA pathogenic variants, of whom 20% (n=1376) had at least one cancer diagnosis, the majority of whom (67%) harbored a BRCA2 pathogenic variant. Median age 52y. Of the 1376 pts with cancer, 83% (n=1144) with 1 cancer, 15% (n=206) with 2 cancers, and 2% (n=26) with 3 independent cancer diagnoses. Any cancer probability (OR 3.2), developing 2 (OR 8.0) or 3 cancers (OR 19.6) were higher with BRCA2. Breast cancer (OR 5.5), Prostate cancer (OR 1.4), Pancreatic cancer (OR 3.0) and CRC (OR 0.5) with BRCA2. All individuals with two independent breast cancers had BRCA2 PV. Non-prostate/breast primaries in 39%, of whom BRCA1 / BRCA2 of 65→ 28%. Driven by CRC (Fig 2). There is likely a role for GnRH agonists, in addition to tamoxifen, for MALEs with breast cancer. QS BRCA1/2 carriers will develop CBC at ~2% per year [Lubinski Br Ca Res Treat '19, van den Broek JCO '16], but this risk is higher for women diagnosed with breast cancer before age 40 [Haffty Lancet '02] and for BRCA1 than BRCA2. This risk is modified by tamoxifen use or oophorectomy [Xu BrCa '15, Metcalfe JCO '04, Pierce JCO '06]. Lifetime CBC risk may be as high as 60-80% among BRCA1/2 carriers [Mavaddat JNCI '13]. Conflicting modern evidence that ppx BSO decreases breast cancer OM [Heemskerk-Gerritsen JNCI '15]. Due to conflicting data for contralateral risk-reducing mastectomy, a cochrane review concluded evidence is insufficient to claim a survival advantage for CRRM [Carbine Cochrane DSR'18]. CRRM does not mandate a SLNB in the context of normal findings on MRI. BRCA1/2 in Locally Recurrent BrCa after BCT [Turner JCO '99]: ± BRCA1/2. Median time to IBTR 5→ 8 years. This suggests BRCA1/2mt may be radiosensitive, as second cancers in the BRCA1/2 cohort occurred in different locations, histology, and timing of subsequent breast events. 10y Multi-institutional results of breast conserving surgery and RT in BRCA1/2 BrCa [Pierce JCO '06]. ± BRCA1/2. Outcomes after BCT for BRCA1/2 are similar if the patient gets BSO (higher recurrence with intact ovaries: Fig 1B), but risk of contralateral BrCa remains high for this high-risk group. Median time to IBTR 5→ 9 years. Second tumors in different quadrants 29→ 60%. WECARE study: CBC after RT Among BRCA1/2 Carriers [Bernstein EJC '13] 603 women with CBC, 1,199 women with unilateral breast cancer with known BRCA status (n=158). RT did not result in a statistically higher risk of CBC in BRCA1/2 carriers. CBC Risk among carriers of germline pathogenic variants in ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, CHEK2, and PALB2 [Yadav JCO '23]: 15,104 prospectively followed women within the CARRIERS study treated with ipsilateral surgery for invasive breast cancer. Germline BRCA1, BRCA2, and CHEK2 PV carriers with breast cancer were at significantly elevated risk (HR > 1.9) of CBC. Only PALB2 PV carriers with ER- breast cancer had elevated risks (HR 2.9) of CBC. African American PV carriers had similarly elevated risks of CBC as non-Hispanic white PV carriers. Among premenopausal women, the 10y cumulative incidence of CBC for CHEK2 / BRCA2 / BRCA1 / PALB2 PV carriers was estimated to be 13→ 27→ 33→ 35%. Among postmenopausal women, the 10y cumulative incidence of CBC for CHEK2 / BRCA2 / BRCA1 / PALB2 PV carriers was estimated to be 4→ 9→ 12%. BRCA1/2 carriers do not have increased acute skin toxicity [Park IJROBP '14]. ATM, CHEK1, ERCC2, RAD51C, TGFB1 are associated with RT-induced early adverse skin reactions. RoR Grade 2+ fibrosis for ± C-509T TGF-β of 4→ 14% [Grossberg JAMA Onc '18]. Non-BRCA hereditary mutations include PALB2, P53, ATM, CHEK2, PTEN, CDH1 and STK11 [Manahan ASO '10]. Homozygous carriers of the ATM gene are exquisitely sensitive, but carriers are only 1-2% of the population. Heterozygous ATM status should not influence decision making regarding RT use. Pathogenic mutation of PALB2 (the partner/localizer of BRCA2) account for < 1% of breast cancers Secondary malignancies are more common with Li-Fraumeni [Wendt Acta Onc '19, Heymann Rad Onc '10]. CHEK21100del have a worse prognosis than CHEK2I157T [Muranen Br Ca Res '16]. Diversified risk: BCAC [NEJM '21] and CARRIERS consortium [Hu NEJM '21]. TBL QS: These large case-control studies expand our understanding of breast cancer susceptibility genes. ATM, BRCA1/2, CHEK2, and PALB2 are most strongly associated with breast cancer. BRCA1/2 and PALB2 associated with the highest absolute risk of breast cancer. ATM and CHEK2 are associated with increased risk of ER+ tumors. BARD1, BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2 and RAD51C/D are associated with increased risk of ER- tumors.

heading: Workup
full_text: Screening (per NCCN 2020.3): Generally speaking, no mammography for women < 30y and no MRI for women < 25y. Clinical encounter and breast awareness starting at age 25. Annual mammogram starting at age 40; no specific age to stop. 5y [Gail model] risk of invasive breast cancer ≥ 1.7%: One of the first tools which attempts to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer over the next 5 years. It includes current age, age of first menstrual period, age at first birth or nulliparity, number of degrees of relatives with a history of breast cancer, number of prior benign breast biopsies, ADH in previous breast biopsy, and race. It may underestimate the need for testing as it does not account for prior ovarian cancer, age of onset of breast cancer, bilateral breast cancers, history of second degree relatives with breast cancers, or the biology of breast cancer. If 5y risk ≥ 1.7% (e.g., LCIS or ADH), may consider risk reduction strategies [NSABP P-1]. RoR May start annual screening MMA younger than age 40. Women with lifetime risk ≥ 20%: Lifetime risk models largely depending on family history: Claus, BRCAPRO, BOADICEA, Tyler-Cuzick. Consider risk reduction strategies. RoR Annual MMA and MRI breast 10y prior to the youngest family member with breast cancer but not prior to age 30 (MMA) or age 25 (MRI). heading: Mammograms
full_text: Imaging in Locoregional Management of Breast Cancer [Kuhl, Lehman and Bedrosian JCO '20]. Zaorsky: [simplified mammography diagram], [mammography interpretations]. 10% are MMA occult. MMA microcalcs are most common (84-98% of cases). Sn and Sp ≥ 90%. Swedish Registry [Duffy Cancer '20]: Registry. ± Mammography screening. Mammography is associated with a 41% reduction in risk of dying of breast cancer within 10 years and a 25% reduction in the rate of advanced breast cancers. 549,091 women, comprising 30% of the Swedish screening-eligible population. Authors calculated an incidence of 2,473 breast cancers that were fatal within 10y after diagnosis and incidence of 9,737 advanced breast cancers. 10y risk of dying of breast cancer RR 0.59. Rate of advanced breast cancers RR 0.75. Screening: MLO for S/I localization. CC for medial-lateral localization. MLO angled 30-60%. Need to see pec muscle to mid-breast/to ensure max breast tissue. Includes ax tail. Diagnostic: Spot compression for masses/densities, magnification view for calcifications ("C for M and M for C"). ~90% of spiculated masses are cancerous, while ~10% of calcifications are cancerous. StatPearls: Breast, Imaging, Reporting and Data System (BI RADS) Last update: 2/17/20. BIRADS 0: Incomplete. 1: Negative. 2: Benign. 3: Probably benign, repeat imaging 6 mo (< 2% risk). 4: Suspicious, biopsy recommended (3-95% risk). 5: Likely cancer (> 95% risk). 6: Biopsy proven mass. UK Age (1990-1997) [Duffy Lanc Onc '20]: Yearly mammography starting at age 50 vs. 40. Yearly mammogram before age 50 is associated with a relative reduction in breast cancer mortality, though this attenuated after 10 years. Reducing the lower age limit for screening from 50 to 40 years could potentially reduce BCM. 160,921 women were randomized from the age of 39-41. Stratified 1:2 by general practice. MFU 23y. 10 year breast cancer deaths 219→ 83 (RR 0.75). After 10 years, breast cancer deaths ~255→ 126 (RR 0.98; IQR 0.8-1.2). False positive rate of 18%. No significant difference in all-cause mortality. Malmo Breast Tomo Screening Trial [Zackrisson Lancet Onc '18]: Tomo vs. 2-view MMA.TBLQS: Single view breast tomosynthesis has a higher sensitivity for detecting breast cancer than two-view digital mammography. To-Be trial [Hofvind Lanc Onc '19]: Tomosynthesis vs. standard digital mammography.TBLQS: Women randomized to first-generation breast tomosynthesis screening had similar cancer detection rates to those who had standard digital mammography. 30,000 women. Recall rate lower with tomo, though rates of biopsy and cancer detection were no different. Tomosynthesis was no better at detecting higher grade tumors. TOSYMA [Heindel Lanc Onc '22]: Digital mammography vs. digital breast tomo + synthesized 2D mammogram. 99,689 women screened from 2018-2020. Invasive breast cancers were detected in 4.8 cases / 7.1 cases per 1000 women screened. Google/DeepMind AI system [McKinney Nature '20]: Radiologist vs. Google/DeepMind. TBLQS: Google and DeepMind’s AI system for mammographic detection of breast cancer performs well—some may point out better than humans—in real-world cohorts of breast cancer screening patients. US: hypoechoic mass with uneven borders, angular margins, taller than wide, and posterior shadowing. Supplemental Breast Cancer-Screening US in Dense Breasts Meta [Yuan BJC '20]: Breast cancer screening by supplemental US among women with dense breasts shows added detection sensitivity compared with MMA alone. However, specificity was slightly decreased. 21 studies included. Pooled Sn of MMA ± US of 74→ 96%. Pooled Sp of MMA ± US of 93→ 87%.

heading: MRI
full_text: Imaging in Locoregional Management of Breast Cancer [Kuhl, Lehman and Bedrosian JCO '20]. MRI supplements MMA beginning at age 30 for patients with high lifetime risk (>20-25% risk): Known BRCA 1/2 or first degree relatives with BRCA1/2 and untested starting at age 25. Lifetime risk > 20-25% [Gail model]: If ≥ 1.7% 5y risk, may consider risk reduction strategies [NSABP P-1]. Prior thoracic RT: Annual MMA and/or MRI 8y after RT, or age 25, whichever is later. Around 25% of mantle field pts treated by age 25 will have breast cancer by age 45 [1]. 1st degree relatives with genetic mutation in TP53 or PTEN (e.g. Cowden, Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba). DENSE trial [Bakker NEJM '19]: Screening MMA ± MRI. TBLQS: Supplemental breast MRI after negative mammogram for women with extremely dense breasts halves the rate of breast cancer that develops in the interval between biennial mammography. 40k pts aged 50-75. Extremely dense breast tissue and normal screening MMA. Interval cancer rate 2.5→ 5 per 1000 screenings. Only 60% received MRI. MRI cancer-detection rate among women who underwent MRI of 16.5 per 1000 screenings. PPV 26% for biopsy. False positive rate 80 per 1000 screenings. FaMRIsc (2011-2017) [Saadatmand Lanc Onc '19]: Screening MMA ± MRI. Biostatistics and Evidence Appraisal For Radiation Oncologists [Rad Onc Seminar Series: Kara Leonard] MRIs are quite helpful to rule out breast cancer, while a positive mammogram has the highest impact on increasing the likelihood of developing breast cancer. 1355 pts. Age 30-55y with cumulative lifetime BrCa risk ≥ 20% but BRCA1/2 and TP53wt. Prior DCIS allowed. Mean number of screening arounds of 4.3. Breast cancer or DCIS detection in 15→ 40 patients. Invasive detection in 8→ 24 patients, size of 1.7→ 0.9 cm, and node positive 63→ 17% (n=5/8, 4/24). Sn ~87→ 98% (p=0.18) Sp 91→ 84%. PPV (BI-RADS ≥ 3) of ~5→ 8% (p=0.07). The accuracy of MRI in determining pCR is 83% [Marinovich JNCI '13]. Imaging to guide NAC: MMA and U/S with correlation coefficients of 0.4, combined 0.7, whereas MRI is 0.8. RoR MRI alters surgical tx in up to 33.3%, may detect occult primary in contralateral breast 3% of the time. Consider for occult primary, assessing response after NAC, multifocal/multicentric disease. Breast MRI should be performed with dedicated breast coil, experienced rads, capacity for MRI-guided bx. Use of Breast MRI at Diagnosis Not Established Fewer re-excisions. Decreased LR. Improved OS. Established Finds multicentric disease in ipsi breast (4-10%, 2B). Screens for contralateral (1-4%, 2B). Evaluation of treatment response after NAC. Occult primary/Paget's. Detect primaries in occult disease (Paget's, axillary primary). More delays, biopsies, and costs. More mastectomies (MRI cohorts are usually younger, denser breasts with larger tumors). MRI detects 98% of cancer and 70% of DCIS. MRI is 98% sensitive for high-grade DCIS, MMA ~50%. MRI does not increase the likelihood of SM- or decrease conversion to mastectomy. MMA microcalcifications are most common. Clumped pattern (vs. heterogeneous) more likely G3, small focal masses associated w ER+ DCIS. >11mm and linear vs grouped more likely to have invasive components. Improved estimate of size that does not correlate entirely with pathology. A01104/ACRIN 6694 [NCT01805076]: ± Preoperative MRI. Will long term local control be improved if additional MRI-detected lesions (4-10%) are removed surgically?

heading: Surgery
full_text: The Landmark Series: Breast Conservation Trials (including oncoplastic breast surgery) [Margenthaler, Dietz and Chatterjee ASO '21] EBCTCG Older BCS and TM Data [Lancet '05]: BCS or TM ± PORT. 5y LRR and 15y CSM. See the [Overview of EBCTCG Studies] section. “The 2005 report on surgery and radiotherapy showed that regimens that substantially reduce 5-year local recurrence rates have little effect on 5-year breast cancer mortality, but moderately reduce 15-year breast cancer mortality.” The 4:1 Rule: Differences in local treatment that substantially affect local recurrence rates would, in the hypothetical absence of any other causes of death, avoid about one breast cancer death over the next 15 years for every four local recurrences avoided, and should reduce 15-year overall mortality.If 5y LR is < 10%, then there is little difference in 15 year BCM.  If 5y LR is > 10%, then BCM is improved. Meta of 42k patients in 78 RCTs. To relate the effect on LRR on BCM, grouping based on 5y LRR ± 10%. BCT to the whole breast, TM to CW and RNI. Around 3/4 of LRR occurred during the first 5y. For BCT, 5y LRR of 26→ 7% (ARR 19%) and 15y CSM of 36→ 30.5% (AMR 5%). For MRM, 5y LRR of 23→ 6% (ARR 17%) and 15y CSM of 60→ 55%. (AMR 5%).Reducing 5y LR by a mean of ~20% reduces the 15y BCM by 5%, regardless of BCS or MRM. 5y tamoxifen decreases LR by ~50% for ER+ disease. Polychemotherapy decreases LR by ~33% depending on age. EBCTCG BCS Data [Lancet '11]: BCS vs. BCT (BCS + WBRT). 10y LRR and 15y CSM See the [Overview of EBCTCG Studies] section. “The 2011 report on radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery showed that radiotherapy halves the rate at which the disease recurs and reduces the breast cancer death rate by about a sixth.” Every four recurrences prevented at 10 years avoids one breast cancer death at 15 years. Modern era data demonstrates a 10y BCM benefit in the context of 10y LRR of 5% [EORTC 22922]. Meta of 10,801 pts in 17 RCTs treated with pN0 and pN+ disease. MFU 9.5y. 10y any first recurrence of 35→ 19% (ARR 16%) and 15y CSM of 25→ 21% (AMR 4%).Overall, about one breast cancer death was avoided by year 15 for every four recurrences avoided by year 10. 10y any recurrence for pN0 subgroups of 31→ 16% (ARR 15%) and 15y CSM of 20→ 17% (AMR 3%). For 10y recurrence reductions of ≥ 20 / 10-20 / < 10%, 15y AMR was 8→ 1→ 0.1%. In other words, there is no survival advantage for 10y ARR < 10% (e.g., lower risk pN0). 10y any recurrence for pN+ subgroup of 64→ 43% (ARR 21%) and 15y CSM of 51→ 43% (AMR 8%). Patients with N1 disease had more pronounced OS benefit than those with N2 disease (DM cause of death). 15y CSM 25→ 21%. RT reduced the annual breast cancer rate by 1/6th. EBCTCG TM Data (1964-1986) [Lancet ‘14]: TM ± PMRT. 10y LRR and 20y CSM. See the [PMRT] section for more. See the [Overview of EBCTCG Studies] section. “The 2014 report showed that after mastectomy, PMRT + RNI reduced breast cancer recurrence and mortality not only in women whose breast cancer had spread to many lymph nodes but also in those with spread to only 1-3 ALNs” There is a suggestion of an overall mortality detriment for pN0 patients who received PMRT. There is a suggestion of a BCM benefit in N1 disease, while an OS benefit was demonstrated for N2 disease. For node positive patients, every 1.5 recurrences prevented by 10y translates to a death avoided at 20 years. Meta of 8k patients on 22 trials from 1964-1986. 3.7k patients were dissected to at least level II. PMRT in all studies included CW, IMN, SCV and/or PAB. Only includes pts median 10 LN removed. Heavily influenced by [Danish trial] which had a large percentage of the total pts (CMF chemo or tamox). PMRT ↓ LR regardless of age, tumor, systemic use, tx era, although ARR was larger in higher risk populations. 10y isolated LRF 21→ 4% and 20y BCM 49→ 41% for all-comers.Overall, about one breast cancer death was avoided by year 20 for every two recurrences avoided by year 10. Oncoplastic Surgery in the Management of Breast Cancer [Shaitelman, Jeruss and Pusic JCO '20]. Nodal harvest: Collects levels I-II (e.g. MRM) Considered full dissection if > 10 LN removed. Include level III only if gross disease in level I or II. Indications for TM: First trimester pregnancy. BCT is reasonable for some 2nd and many 3rd trimester patients who can receive RT after delivery. Diffuse microcalcifications on imaging, multicentric DCIS (20-30% of TM specimens have multicentric disease). Prior RT to chest wall or breast. Unattainable negative margins. Large tumor size relative to small breast size. DCIS is associated with BRCA mutations (patients may elect for b/l MRM). Contraindications to BCS: Absolute: Pregnancy (cannot do SLNB/radioactive dye), persistent SM+ (e..g. Multicentric or multifocal), diffuse microcalcifications, multicentric (now more of a relative contraindication and the subject of Alliance Z11102 [NCT01556243]RoR), homozygous for ATM mutation. Relative: Prior RT, active scleroderma/lupus, T3+, focally SM+, genetic/suspected predisposition to breast cancer, large breast to tumor ratio, known genetic predisposition. Outcomes after BCT for BRCA1/2 are similar if pt gets BSO (higher recurrence with intact ovaries); no increased toxicity from RT; however, BRCA1/2 patients remain at higher risk of contralateral BrCa [Pierce JCO '06]. The use of cavity shave margins are associated with lower re-excision rates, more than surgeon characteristics, practice setting, or other surgical techniques [Chakedis JAMA Netw Open '22]. QS There may be increased CSS/OS with BCT as opposed to TM [van Maaren Lanc Onc '16, Agarwal JAMA Surg '14]. ACOSOG Z11102 (2012-2016) [Boughey JCO '23]: Phase II. Multi-focal (2-3 lesions)→ BCT with WBRT. 270 women ≥ 40y with 2-3 foci of biopsy-proven cN0-1 breast cancer, 204 eligible. Primary endpoint of 5y LR with an a priori rate of clinical acceptability of < 8%. MFU 5.5y. 5y LR 3% (95% CI 1.3-6.4%). 5y LR for ± pre-op MRI exploratory analysis of 23→ 2%. Types of Mastectomy: Radical (Halsted Mastectomy): Pec minor/major + levels I-III. Modified Radical Mastectomy: Underlying fascia of pec major + levels I-II. Spares pectoralis muscle. Complete removal of breast tissue = Tissue inferior to axillary v from lat dorsi to med border of pec minor. Removal of Breast from clavicle to rectus abdominis and sternal edge and lat dorsi. Pec Minor and Pec Major are preserved (sometimes pec minor can be removed). Intercostobrachial nerve is sacrificed→ numbness in the medial arm. Total (Simple) Mastectomy: Only used for ppx or DCIS. No ALND. Skin sparing Mastectomy: Majority of skin left for reconstruction. Nipple sparing Mastectomy: Can spare the nipple if DCIS >2 cm from the nipple; early stage biologically favorable. Oncoplastic volume displacement aka mastopexy to fill the void. Quadrantectomy: Tumor + 1.5-2 cm with overlying skin and deep muscle fascia. Bernard Fisher: 1918-2019 [Wolmark JCO '20]: See [NSABP Studies: An Overview]. What follows is a hopeless simplification of this article. Every oncologist should read it. "A Turtle only makes progress when its head is exposed" "In God we trust; all others must have data". "[NSABP B-04] had an enormous influence on how surgeons and clinicians perceived the behavior of breast cancer; it convinced them, once and for all, that nuances in locoregional therapy were unlikely to have a substantial influence on ultimate survival and that patients succumbed to the disease not because of inattention to operative detail but rather because micrometastases were present at the time of the initial operation. This provided the biologic rationale for the evolution of clinical trials that evaluated not only additional reduction in the extent of locoregional therapy, but also, more importantly, the use of adjuvant systemic therapy. The retreat from radical mastectomy and the ascent of systemic therapy are inextricably intertwined." "NSABP B-04 proved to be the elusive Rosetta Stone that ushered in a Periclean age of clinical trials. The findings enabled the development of ensuing clinical trials showing that breast-preserving operations ([NSABP B-06]; reported 1985) were the equivalent of the TM and the first demonstration that adjuvant chemo could prolong DFS (NSABP B-05; reported 1975). Subsequent clinical trials, namely B-09 (reported 1981) and [B-14] (reported 1989), established that the use of tamoxifen in patients whose tumors contained estrogen receptors was salutary in both node-positive and node-negative breast cancer." "In 1988, the assault on the radical mastectomy continued with the initiation of the first clinical trial to evaluate the worth of preoperative chemotherapy in stage I and II breast cancer [NSABP B-18]. The implementation of preoperative chemotherapy was a direct confrontation to the primacy of operative intervention" "In 1992, an ambitious initiative was launched to determine whether tamoxifen could prevent the subsequent occurrence of breast cancer in women who were considered at high risk of developing the disease. [NSABP P-01] randomly assigned 13,388 women without breast cancer to tamoxifen or to placebo. The results of this trial, first reported in 1997,10 confirmed that tamoxifen could reduce the subsequent incidence of invasive breast cancer by approximately 50%. Bernard Fisher considered the trials demonstrating the benefit of tamoxifen in the preventive and therapeutic adjuvant settings to be the cornerstones of his legacy." Why are Mastectomies no longer needed? See [NSABP Studies: An Overview] and the Summary Box on Bernard Fisher above. BCS has equivalent OS, CSS and DM as compared to TM [NSABP B-06]. Results of prospective RCTs comparing reduced extent of surgery: Three trials with equivalent LRC when BCT compared to MRM. There was equivalent CBC and second non-breast malignancies. There is no modern study comparing MRM to BCS, and we will never have one. Both Milan I and EORTC 10801 demonstrate increased local failure with reduced extent of surgery. NSABP B-04 (25y) [Flowchart, Fisher Cancer '77, NEJM '02]: cN0. RM vs. TM ± regional PORT if cN0, mandated if cN+. See the [Overview of NSABP Studies] section for more. Caveat: No systemic therapy given in B-04. TM + PMRT is just as effective as the Halsted. Paved way for BCS.Of women cN0 axilla without nodal dissection or PORT, 20% eventually developed a clinically positive axilla. 1079 pts. Women cN0 who had TM alone (no ALND) with subsequent axillary nodes allowed to have ALND. RT: If regional PORT is given (cN+, cN0 if randomized), then PAB fields were used as it is an older trial. cN+ (2 arm): RM vs. TM + regional PORT. There was an equivalent DFS/OS. cN0 (3 arm): RM vs. TM ± regional PORT (these old trials used PAB). There was an equivalent DFS/OS. Of cN0 arms, axillary failure for TM alone (no ALND) / RM of 19→ < 4%. Axillary LND was eventually performed if LN became positive without evidence of distant mets. Median time from mastectomy to identification of axillary nodes of 15 mo. NSABP B-06 (20y; 1976-1984) [Flowchart, Fisher NEJM '85, '89, '02]: BCS ± WBRT vs TM. ALND in all. See the [Overview of NSABP Studies] section for more. BCS + XRT is equivalent to TM in terms of OS, at the cost of marginally more local recurrences.Don't forget about the small DCIS cohort in this trial! Notable NSABP DCIS trials: B-06, B-17, B-24. 1843 pts. Stage I/II IDC (< 4 cm). Positive nodes received adjuvant 5-FU based chemo. WBRT: 50 Gy without RNI or a boost. DCIS ['86, '91] in 75 pts: LR for BCS / BCT / TM of 43→ 7→ 4%. 20y OS ~46%. 20y IBTR for BCS / BCT of 39→ 14% (does not include a boost). EORTC 10801 (20y; 1980-1986) [Litière Lanc Onc '12]: TM vs. BCT + boost. There is no difference in DM or OS with BCT versus MRM. LC is similar when accounting for SM+ with BCT. 902 pts. Stage I/II IDC, < 5 cm. Negative SM were not required - 48% were SM+. Chemo given if N+ and < 55yo. WBRT: 50/25 with 25 Gy Ir-192 boost. 22y DM ~45%. 12y OS ~66%. 10y LF 12→ 20%. Milan I (20y; 1973-1980) [Veronesi NEJM '02]: RM vs. BCT (quadrantectomy). ALND in all. Equivalent CSS and OS at 20 years of follow up. The incidence of new cancers ipsilateral breast in a location other than the index lesion was similar to that observed in the contralateral breast. This suggests that elective treatment of the remaining ipsilateral breast may not be necessary. This fact was used as the basis in the discussion for [NSABP B-39], an APBI trial. 701 pts. Stage I/II IDC < 70y. 60 Gy BCT. Later on, N+ pts had CMF chemo. 20y LF 2→ 9%. 20y OS ~59%, 20y CSS ~75%. BCT and reduction of LRR for IDC Around 2/3 RRR in LR with RT for IDC! Compare to 1/2 RRR in LR for DCIS per [EBCTCG].
